name: Delegation chains for demand-side grants
description: Cross-SDK vectors for the delegation-chain rule in L2 Grants in trust records, which is experimental in 3.3 (adcontextprotocol/adcp#8118, P7). Each vector gives an acts-for claim and the trust records that each registrable domain publishes, and the seller's expected outcome. `input.brand` is `account.brand`. `input.parent_organization` is the parent organization that brand.json resolves, or null for a standalone brand. `input.signer.operator` is the signer's operator, and `input.signer.origin` is the signer's canonical origin. `input.trust_records` maps each registrable domain to the `grants` and `exclusive_grants` of its trust.json; a domain that is absent publishes no grants. All domains are registrable domains already, so no Public Suffix List lookup is needed, and every record is fetched. `expected.outcome` is one of `implicit`, `authorized`, `grant_absent`, or `seller_discretion`. When no delegation chain covers the claim, the outcome is `grant_absent` if the parent organization's record sets `exclusive_grants: true`, and `seller_discretion` otherwise: the seller's own onboarding records decide. `expected` holds the outcome only. Each vector tests one premise: every other premise of the claim holds, so an implementation fails a vector only when it gets that premise wrong, whatever order it checks the premises in. Look up vectors by `id`; `description` prose may change.

vectors.description: The parent organization grants the agency, and the agency operates the account and signs with its own agent.
The brand operates its account through an agent that a platform hosts. The parent organization grants the platform.
The parent organization grants the agency, and the agency grants the platform that hosts the signing agent. The narrowing is on the second grant.
The parent organization grants the agency twice. The first grant covers governance only, and the second covers media buying, so the second grant authorizes. Every grant in grants[] is a candidate.
The agency grants the platform twice. The first grant covers governance only, and the second covers media buying, so the delegation chain runs through the second.
The parent organization operates the account through an agent that a platform hosts, and grants the platform directly. No grant to itself is needed.
The parent organization operates the account, grants the agency, and the agency grants the platform. The rule admits this combination.
The brand operates the account, the parent organization grants the agency, and the agency grants the platform. The rule admits this combination.
The brand operates the account and signs with its own agent. Authority is implicit, and the exclusive record without a grant to the brand does not matter.
The parent organization operates the account and signs with its own agent. Authority is implicit.
The brand operates the account, and the parent organization signs with its own agent. Each is the brand or its parent organization, so authority is implicit.
The parent organization operates the account, and the brand signs with its own agent. Each is the brand or its parent organization, so authority is implicit.

The brand signs with its own agent, but the account names the agency as its operator. Implicit authority needs the brand or the parent organization as both the account operator and the signer's operator.
A brand with no parent organization authorizes from its own record.

A brand with no parent organization publishes an exclusive record that grants the agency governance only. The brand has no separate parent organization, so its own exclusive_grants counts and the media-buying claim is denied.
The platform grants a relay a third time. A delegation chain has at most two grants, so the relay's agent is not covered.

The parent organization grants the brand, the brand grants the agency, and the agency grants the platform. The brand operates the account. A delegation chain has at most two grants, even when the brand is a middle grantee, so the platform's agent is not covered.
The parent organization grants the platform, but the account names an agency that is neither the brand, the parent organization, nor the first grantee.
The account names the platform, which is the grantee of the second grant. account.operator must be the brand, the parent organization, or the grantee of the first grant.
The first grant covers governance only, so it does not cover the media-buying claim. The second grant covers it.
The first grant covers a different brand the parent organization owns. The second grant covers the account's brand.
The first grant covers CA only, and the account's brand covers the US. The second grant is global.
The check time is before the first grant's valid_from. The second grant is already valid.
The second grant is still valid, but the check time is at or after the first grant's valid_until.
The first grant lists only the agency's own agents, so it never covers the platform's agent, even though the agency grants the platform.
The second grant covers governance only, so it does not cover the media-buying claim. The first grant covers it.
The second grant covers a different brand. The first grant covers the account's brand.
The account's brand covers GB. The second grant covers CA and the US only, so it doesn't cover the brand's countries.
The first grant is still valid, but the check time is before the second grant's valid_from.
The check time is at or after the second grant's valid_until. The first grant is still valid.
The second grant lists only another of the platform's agents, so the signer's canonical origin is not listed. The first grant is unnarrowed.
The check time equals the grant's valid_until. A grant is inactive at or after valid_until, so it doesn't cover the claim.
The check time equals the grant's valid_from. A grant is active from valid_from on, so it covers the claim.
The account's brand lists no countries, and the grant covers the US only. A brand reference with no countries is covered only by a global grant.
The account's brand reference has no brand_id, and the grant lists specific brands. A brand reference with no brand_id is covered only by ["*"] or an omitted list.
The grant covers a different brand the parent organization owns.
The grant lists ["*"] as its brands, which covers every brand the parent organization owns.
The parent organization's exclusive record grants the platform governance only. No grant covers media buying, and the record is the complete list for every scope, so the claim is denied.
The grant lists ["*"] as its scopes. The bare token * covers every scope in every namespace, so it covers the media-buying claim.
The brand's own record grants the platform, but only the parent organization's record authorizes, and it grants the agency only.
The brand's own record is exclusive and grants another domain, but the parent organization's record grants the platform.
The parent organization grants the brand, and the brand operates the account. The brand's own record supplies the second grant, to the platform that hosts the signing agent.
The parent organization's exclusive record lists no grants, so no third party acts for it.
The parent organization's record is not exclusive and grants the platform governance only. No delegation chain covers the platform's media-buying claim, so the seller's onboarding records decide.
The parent organization's nonexclusive record grants the agency media buying for another brand it owns. The grant covers nothing for this brand and doesn't narrow the seller's discretion.

The brand's own record is exclusive and lists no grants, and the parent organization's record is not exclusive. Only the parent organization's exclusive_grants counts, so a claim that no delegation chain covers stays at the seller's discretion.

The agency's own record is exclusive, and the parent organization's record is not. The second grant covers governance only, so no delegation chain covers the media-buying claim. Only the parent organization's exclusive_grants counts, so the claim stays at the seller's discretion.
